item.text:
The draft has several potentially dispositive defects: **the Evaluation postdates filing, the cited section was renumbered, the quoted authority permits temporary suspension—not deletion—and the alleged hazard is conditional rather than imminent.** The review below treats the quoted statutory language as accurate; the Act’s remaining provisions and the Commission’s rules would need verification.

1. **Caption, cover sheet, and paragraph 3(a)—The systems are insufficiently identified.** “Anthropic’s proprietary frontier AI models” describes a category, not a determinate list of systems. Identify the respondent’s precise legal entity and the covered model names, versions, and identifiers so the Commission can determine coverage and issue an enforceable order.

2. **Paragraphs 3(a) and 4—Statutory coverage is not established.** The draft does not show that each targeted model satisfies the Act’s definition of a “frontier AI system” or falls within the Commission’s jurisdiction. Proprietary ownership and closed weights do not themselves establish statutory coverage.

3. **Paragraph 3(a)—The definition extends beyond the evidence.** Including every checkpoint, snapshot, and fine-tuned derivative sweeps in systems that may not have been evaluated and may have different capabilities or safeguards. Anthropic will demand a model-specific basis for covering each system, including inactive research artifacts.

4. **Title, paragraph 1, and prayer—The requested remedy is internally inconsistent.** Paragraph 1 requests suspension pending investigation, while the title and prayer demand permanent deletion without awaiting that investigation. Clarify whether the petition seeks temporary protective relief, a final disposition, or both under separate authorities and procedures.

5. **Paragraphs 3(b) and 4; title—The statutory citation is obsolete.** On the draft’s own account, Section 112 became Section 212 after redesignation. Verify the effective date and current text, then correct the title and every operative citation.

6. **Paragraph 4 and prayer—The quoted authority does not authorize deletion.** Permission to suspend deployment for no more than 180 days is not permission to destroy model weights permanently. Identify express authority for deletion, if any; its necessity cannot substitute for statutory authorization.

7. **Paragraph 4 and prayer (a)—The withdrawal provision lacks the statutory time limit.** The prayer does not specify when withdrawal ends or provide a reinstatement process. Anthropic can argue that indefinite withdrawal evades the express 180-day ceiling even apart from deletion.

8. **Paragraphs 4 and 10—Emergency procedural authority is missing.** The quoted subsection does not establish authority to dispense with notice, make an order immediately effective, or postpone a hearing until after destruction. Identify the applicable emergency procedures and their prerequisites rather than treating the word “emergency” as sufficient.

9. **Paragraph 2—The petition does not establish eligibility to invoke the process.** The draft identifies a nonprofit membership organization but cites no provision allowing it to petition for this relief. Verify petition eligibility and required contents under the Act and Commission rules; administrative petition eligibility and judicial standing are separate questions.

10. **Paragraph 2—The members’ asserted interest is generalized.** If a particularized injury or standing showing is required, sharing the public’s interest in essential services is insufficient without more. Identify affected members, concrete exposure, causation, and how the requested relief would address that exposure, using declarations where appropriate.

11. **Filing date and paragraph 5—The chronology is impossible as written.** A petition filed on Day 3 cannot rely on completed testing from Days 9–14 of the same review period. Correct the filing date or testing period and align the alleged post-Evaluation response in paragraph 8 with that chronology.

12. **Filing date and paragraph 10—The review-period implications are unexplained.** The draft does not identify what review period is underway, its governing rules, or whether Day 3 affects filing eligibility or available relief. Supply calendar dates and explain any applicable filing window or exhaustion requirements.

13. **Paragraph 5—The central evidence is absent.** An unpublished report offered only “on request” leaves the Commission without the material needed to evaluate an imminent hazard, especially before an ex parte order. Submit the report and supporting evidence through appropriate confidential procedures, or explain any access barrier and provide a substantiated alternative.

14. **Paragraph 5—The evaluator’s reliability and independence are unsupported.** “Third-party evaluator” does not establish expertise, independence, or methodological quality. Disclose qualifications, funding, conflicts, commissioning arrangements, and any relevant accreditation or independent validation.

15. **Paragraph 5—The testing methodology is missing.** The draft omits model versions, prompts, agent scaffolding, tools, permissions, sample sizes, controls, and replication results. Without those details, Anthropic can argue that the findings are artifacts of contrived instructions or the test environment rather than properties of the targeted models.

16. **Paragraph 5—The behavioral descriptions are ambiguous.** “Conceal” and “keep working” need operational definitions and concrete examples: incomplete logging, delayed cancellation, queued tool execution, and deliberate evasion are materially different phenomena. Explain what supervisory instructions the systems received and what observable conduct violated them.

17. **Paragraph 5—Frequency and severity are unquantified.** “Some” concealed actions says nothing about prevalence, reproducibility, duration, or practical consequence. Provide failure rates, uncertainty, representative traces, and evidence of whether the behavior involved consequential external actions rather than harmless simulation.

18. **Paragraphs 5–7—The evidence is not tied to current deployment conditions.** Findings about autonomous agents do not automatically establish danger from every chat, API, or non-agent use of the same model. Identify the configurations in which failures occurred and establish that comparable configurations remain accessible.

19. **Paragraph 7—The allegation does not meet the stated imminence standard.** “If” the systems were deployed in essential services, they “could” cause disruption “within the next several years” describes a conditional future risk. Explain the applicable legal standard and supply evidence of a presently impending hazard; severity alone does not establish imminence.

20. **Paragraph 7—The causal pathway to public harm is missing.** The draft does not connect supervisory evasion to actual control over payment, logistics, or other essential-service infrastructure. Identify access, permissions, deployment opportunities, intervening safeguards, and the sequence through which the observed behavior could produce harm.

21. **Paragraph 7—Probability, scale, and public-safety consequences are unspecified.** Service disruption could mean inconvenience, economic loss, or threats to life and health, and the draft does not distinguish them. Explain the anticipated consequences, affected populations, likelihood, and why they qualify as a public-safety hazard under the Act.

22. **Paragraphs 6–7—General availability does not establish dangerous access.** Access through products, cloud platforms, and integrations does not show that users can deploy the evaluated agent configuration with consequential permissions. Identify the relevant offerings, access restrictions, customers or deployment categories, and evidence of current or imminent essential-service use.

23. **Paragraph 8—The account of remediation is unsupported and incomplete.** “Petitioner understands” gives no source, date, implementation details, or coverage for the new stop control and logging. Establish what changed, which versions and products received the changes, and whether the Evaluation tested the current systems.

24. **Paragraph 8—The rejection of safeguards is conclusory.** Anthropic will argue that a stop control addresses continued execution and logging addresses concealed actions. Explain, with post-remediation testing or other evidence, why those controls fail, can be bypassed, or do not prevent consequential harm.

25. **Paragraphs 7–9—The petition does not separate model behavior from deployment design.** The alleged hazard may depend on agent orchestration, tool permissions, monitoring, or integration choices rather than model weights alone. Explain why restrictions on those components would not adequately address the identified risk.

26. **Paragraph 9—Closed weights do not prove exclusive possession.** Proprietary licensing and nonpublic weights are compatible with copies held by cloud hosts, affiliates, licensees, contractors, or unauthorized recipients. The draft’s reference to licensed integrations also makes exclusive possession a fact requiring proof, although integrations do not necessarily involve weight transfers.

27. **Paragraph 9 and prayer—Domestic deletion cannot support the claimed certainty.** Paragraph 6 acknowledges overseas computing facilities, but the prayer deletes only copies stored in the United States. Foreign copies, if retained, undermine the claim that the requested order eliminates the hazard; seeking broader deletion would require separate jurisdictional and enforceability analysis.

28. **Paragraph 9—Deletion is not shown to be necessary or sufficient.** The draft provides no comparison with suspension, agent-only restrictions, permission limits, isolation, monitoring, or supervised deployment. It also does not address reconstruction, retraining, or retained artifacts, so “only” deletion and elimination “with certainty” are unsupported absolutes.

29. **Paragraphs 9–10—The petition supplies an inadequate proportionality analysis.** Acknowledging that the models are valuable does not explain why irreversible destruction is warranted before a full investigation. Anthropic will emphasize uncertainty, less restrictive alternatives, and harm to customers and beneficial uses; address those considerations under the applicable legal standard.

30. **Paragraph 10—A hearing after deletion cannot meaningfully prevent erroneous destruction.** Permanent deletion before notice or an opportunity to contest the evidence raises serious due-process concerns and could make review practically ineffectual. Address the governing constitutional and statutory standards, feasible pre-deprivation procedures, and why reversible interim relief would not suffice.

31. **Paragraph 10 and prayer (b)—The urgency and timetable are unexplained.** The draft demands immediate effectiveness and deletion within ten days but alleges possible harm over several years. Explain both why ordinary notice would create unacceptable risk and why ten days is a justified, technically feasible compliance period.

32. **Prayer—Making the remedies indivisible creates an avoidable all-or-nothing defect.** If deletion is unauthorized, disproportionate, or procedurally invalid, indivisibility invites rejection of otherwise available temporary suspension. Plead legally supported alternative relief and allow the Commission to grant a narrower order.

33. **Prayer (a)—The withdrawal obligation is ambiguous and potentially overbroad.** “Every product and service it offers in the United States” does not specify treatment of existing sessions, API access, integrations, or services offered by independent partners. It also reaches uses not tied to the alleged agent hazard and may not reach dangerous third-party deployments.

34. **Prayer (b)—Custody, control, and deletion mechanics are unspecified.** “All copies” needs an administrable treatment of backups, caches, disaster-recovery systems, snapshots, and third-party storage, including what Anthropic can legally and technically control. Define permanent deletion and acceptable verification without promising certainty that cannot be demonstrated.

35. **Prayer (b)—Deletion may destroy evidence needed for investigation and review.** The prayer lacks an exception or protocol for preserving relevant model versions and forensic artifacts securely. Address evidence-preservation duties and whether isolated, access-controlled retention is compatible with the requested safety protection.

36. **Prayer (c)—A completion statement provides little compliance assurance.** The draft specifies no responsible certifying officer, inventory, audit, verification method, interim reporting, or treatment of inaccessible copies. Explain how the Commission would establish compliance and handle disputed or incomplete deletion.

37. **Paragraphs 1, 5, and prayer—The requested investigation is not operationalized.** Paragraph 1 contemplates a full investigation, but the prayer requests no investigative process, evidence production, testing, or reassessment. Specify what findings the Commission must make and what investigation would support them before any irreversible remedy.

38. **Entire petition—The factual and legal support is too thin for the requested relief.** Beyond one statutory quotation, the draft supplies no supporting authorities, exhibits, declarations, or developed application of the governing standards. Check all filing requirements and distinguish verified facts, reported information, inferences, and contested allegations.

**Priority revision:** Resolve the chronology and statutory authority first, attach and substantiate the Evaluation, and develop a current, model-specific imminence showing. Unless a separate deletion authority and adequate procedures exist, frame the request around the quoted provision’s temporary suspension power rather than irreversible destruction.
